### 1972. The Positioning Era Cometh

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/history-of-advertising/1972-the-positioning-era/
Date: 2026-08-19. Read: 10 min.

In April 1972 Ries and Trout told Advertising Age the battleground had moved to the prospect's mind. What Avis, Volkswagen and 7-Up had proved, and what to do now.

## The moment

Monday 24 April 1972. Advertising Age, page 35. Two account men from a small New York agency, Al Ries and Jack Trout, open a three-part series with a sentence written to annoy every creative department on Madison Avenue: "Today it has become obvious that advertising is entering a new era. An era where creativity is no longer the key to success." [2] The second part runs on 1 May, the third on 8 May. The series is called "The Positioning Era Cometh". Its claim fits on an index card. The battleground has moved out of the product and into the prospect's mind. The campaigns that prove it are a decade old, and the industry already knows them by heart.

## What came before

Trout had used the word first, in June 1969, in the trade magazine Industrial Marketing, under a title nobody would choose today: "'Positioning' is a game people play in today's me-too market place". The idea was already whole. "Positioning is a game where the competitor's image is just as important as your own. Sometimes more important." [1] Few noticed. Ries gave a speech on it at the Sales Executives Club of New York; Rance Crain, the editor of Advertising Age, heard it and asked for a series. The book, Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind, came in 1981.

The series told the industry's history as three eras. The product era of the 1950s, Rosser Reeves and the [unique selling proposition](/principles/unique-selling-proposition/), ended under an avalanche of me-too products. The image era of the 1960s belonged to David Ogilvy. The third they dated to a full-page Ogilvy advertisement in the New York Times on 7 April 1971, 38 points on advertising that sells, the first of which read "The results of your campaign depend less on how we write your advertising than on how your product is positioned." [2] The architect of one era, they wrote, had called the tune for the next. The word, then, is Trout's. The practice belongs to the people who wrote Avis and Volkswagen. The theory is the series.

## What it changed

The argument rested on a count. Ries and Trout wrote that per-capita advertising consumption in the United States was "approaching $100 a year", that the average mind met "more than half a million advertising messages" a year and, citing George Miller, could hold about seven items in a category at once [2]. The first checks out; the other two we take on the authors' word. Robert Coen's historical series puts total US advertising at $12.0 billion in 1960 and $23.2 billion in 1972, which over a population of a little more than 200 million is their $100 [5]. Television took the growth: $1.6 billion in 1960, $4.1 billion in 1972, $11.5 billion by 1980 [5].

The money followed the screen. Nine per cent of US households had a television set in 1950. By 1960 it was 87%, by 1972 96% [6]. Ries and Trout measured the crowding in one line: "In 1964, there were seven soft drinks advertised on network television. Today there are 22." [2]

Print stood still. Daily newspaper circulation was 58.9 million in 1960 and 62.2 million in 1980, while the advertising inside those papers quadrupled, from $3.7 billion to $14.8 billion [5][6]. More messages, the same heads.

The day before, an agency's job was to find something true about the product and say it well. The day after, the job started with what the prospect already believed about the category and its leader. "The mind accepts only that new information which matches its prior knowledge or experience. It filters out everything else." [2] Avis's line worked because Hertz was already in the head, and Avis attached itself to it. Seven-Up's "Un-Cola" worked because two out of three soft drinks sold in America were colas; the cola slot was full, the slot beside it was empty, and sales rose "something like 10%" in the first year, by the authors' account [2]. Beck's set itself against Löwenbräu as the German beer Germans drink. Schaefer took "the one beer to have when you're having more than one", and Honeywell, in its own advertising, called itself "the other computer company vs. Mr. Big" and let IBM keep the lead [2].

Two consequences followed. The strategist moved ahead of the writer. And awards stopped counting as evidence. Of 41 agencies that had won Hall of Fame Clios, the series noted, 31 had since lost some or all of the accounts concerned [2]. "The fun and games of the '60s have given way to the harsh realities of the '70s." [2]

The modern test is less kind than the authors were. Romaniuk, Sharp and Ehrenberg asked the buyers of brands in 17 categories across Australia and the UK whether the brand they used was "different" or "unique". On average, 17% said either [7]. Buyers can see a large difference when one exists, 67% of Aldi's own shoppers and 50% of Subway's said so; Coca-Cola at 19% and Apple at 23% do not come close [7]. The memory half of positioning survived the test. The difference half failed it.

## The Mad Men thread

The series on AMC runs from March 1960 to November 1970 [19]. Positioning arrives eighteen months after the finale, and the campaigns it was built on are the ones the fictional Sterling Cooper watches from across the street. Third episode, 1960: the creative team passes round a Volkswagen ad from Doyle Dane Bernbach, Don Draper dislikes it, Pete Campbell calls it brilliant.

The record is better than the script. DDB opened on 1 June 1949, Ned Doyle, Maxwell Dane and Bill Bernbach, and its method was, in Mark Tungate's words, "copywriters and art directors working side by side" from the first idea [9]. Volkswagen gave DDB its US account in 1959, with Helmut Krone as art director and Julian Koenig as writer, and "Think small" and "Lemon" came out of that pairing.

Robert Townsend arrived at Avis from American Express early in 1962 and hired DDB. By Time's account, the agency asked what Avis did better than Hertz, and on cars, locations and rates the answer was nothing. "Well," said Townsend, "we try harder." [10]

Paula Green wrote the campaign and Krone laid it out. By mid-1964 the fleet had gone from 16,600 cars to 36,000 and rentals were up 28% [10].

Mary Wells was copy chief at DDB in 1963, moved to Jack Tinker & Partners in 1964, repainted Braniff's aircraft under the line "The End of the Plain Plane" with Richard Rich and Stewart Greene, and founded Wells Rich Greene with them in April 1966. George Lois had left DDB in January 1960 to co-found Papert Koenig Lois with Julian Koenig; Steven Heller called PKL "the second creative agency in the world" [18].

What the series showed is a composite. The Kodak Carousel, Jaguar and Burger Chef pitches are inventions; the finale closes on McCann Erickson's real 1971 Coca-Cola film. The revolution happened at DDB, PKL, Tinker and Wells Rich Greene. Positioning came after it, and its authors' nerve ran ahead of their data. They predicted that Avis, now boasting, would lose ground to Hertz and National, and that Volkswagen, which had run "Think small" one year and announced a big Volkswagen the next, would erode fast. Volkswagen of America's sales fell from about 570,000 vehicles in 1970 to just under 486,000 in 1972 [11]. Whether Avis lost ground we could not settle; the share figures in circulation contradict one another.

## Applied: if you are a B2C brand

Say you sell a sparkling water in a market where two giants hold most of the shelf and most of the heads. Start from what the buyer already knows about those two. Avis conceded the rank and turned it into a reason. Seven-Up let the colas keep the category and named itself by them. Your version only makes sense because the giants exist, the water defined by what it is not. Write it in one line, and if that line only works for a buyer who already knows you, start again.

Then add the later evidence. Across 17 categories, only 17% of a brand's own buyers call it different or unique, and they buy it anyway [7]. So spend the budget on recall. One bottle and one line, repeated until the trade is tired of them, in front of every category buyer the money reaches. The Uncola's deepest asset was the word, and the years Seven-Up left it alone.

## Applied: if you are a B2B brand

Say you sell a project management platform in a category with one dominant incumbent, and your buyers are operations directors who already run it. Ries and Trout would have you own a word. Honeywell took "the other computer company" and let IBM keep "computers" [2]. The word you can own is the one the incumbent cannot say without contradicting itself. If the incumbent is the suite IT chose for everyone, your word is the tool the operations director chose for her own team.

Keller's discipline comes first, though. Before the point of difference, list the points of parity, the features "brands have in common with competitors" on which you only need to break even, such as security certifications and the integrations on the buyer's checklist [8]. Then decide what to own. A word is a claim the buyer must accept. A distinctive asset, in Ehrenberg-Bass's sense, is a colour or a shape that only has to be recognised. Own both and measure them separately. Ask whether buyers can name your word unprompted, and whether they can name your brand from the asset alone. We would bet the second number moves first.

## What to do with it

1. Write the position as one sentence that names the leader or the category. Delete the leader's name and read it again; if the sentence still holds, you have written a product description. 2. Find the slot that is already open. List the words buyers attach to the leader; your position is the word on that list the leader cannot take, or the honest rank the leader cannot claim. 3. Settle parity before difference. Write the three to five things every supplier in your category must have, confirm you have each one, and only then write a line about what makes you different. 4. Test recall first. Ask 100 category buyers to name your brand from your line, colour or shape alone; separately, ask your own buyers whether the brand is different or unique, and compare that with the 17% norm [7] before spending to move it. 5. Hold the position for five years. Volkswagen's lesson in 1972 was that one year of "Big" was enough for two consultants to predict erosion in print. Before approving a new campaign, put it beside the last one and ask whether a buyer who saw the last would know it is the same brand.

### 1994. The first banner ad

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/history-of-advertising/1994-the-first-banner-ad/
Date: 2026-08-14. Read: 10 min.

HotWired ran the first banners on 27 October 1994. What the 44 per cent click rate and the fall to 0.1 per cent mean for your display budget.

## The moment

27 October 1994, South Park, San Francisco. A dozen people stand around a server in the office of HotWired, the web arm of Wired magazine. Brian Behlendorf throws the switch. The site crashes under its first traffic and comes back up [2]. Above the content on each section sit rectangles 468 pixels wide and 60 deep, a dozen or so of them, for AT&T, MCI, Volvo, Club Med, Zima, Sprint, IBM and 1-800-Collect. The AT&T one, written by Joe McCambley at Modem Media and designed by Craig Kanarick, reads: "Have you ever clicked your mouse right here? You will." Click it and you land on a page of museum websites, the Louvre among them.

## What came before

The problem HotWired solved was money. Andrew Anker, who wrote its business plan in March 1994, said later that the site's decisions "were really not brilliant decisions, they were constraints": there was no secure way to take a credit card online, so advertisers were the only people who could pay [1]. Louis Rossetto, Wired's co-founder, was told that if he sold ads the internet would throw up on him. He did it anyway.

The model was print. A page in Wired cost about $10,000, so HotWired charged $10,000 a month for the sponsorship of one section [2]. Rick Boyce, who built the first web ad sales team, remembers the launch price as twelve weeks for $30,000, with no traffic guarantee and no promise about clicks. There was no ad server, so ads were hard-coded into their sections and staff parsed the web logs by hand. Most advertisers had no website to send a click to.

There was no single first banner. Digiday counts twelve brands and Wired fourteen, all live the same morning, and AT&T's is remembered because it was the best known and, by its makers' account, the best performing [3]. Neither count is settled. What HotWired did first was sell a measured space to a national advertiser and report the response back.

## What it changed

The ad could be counted. For the first time a marketer could know how many people saw an ad and how many acted on it [3]. The first numbers were absurd. McCambley recalls the AT&T banner's click rate in the high 70s for two or three weeks, then settling "in the 40s" for two months, 44 per cent being the figure AT&T's Bill Clausen gave him [1]. Anker's rule for the rest of 1994 and well into 1995 was that any banner below 2 per cent was a bad banner. Those rates belonged to novelty and a small, curious audience: 14 per cent of American adults had internet access in 1995 [16].

Standard sizes followed, and with them a middleman. On 10 December 1996 the Internet Advertising Bureau, founded that June, and CASIE, a task force of the advertisers' and agencies' associations, published eight voluntary banner sizes, because more than 250 were in use and agencies were being asked for ads "in 50 or more sizes" [6]. DoubleClick, which began as a division of the Poppe Tyson agency in 1995 and merged with Kevin O'Connor and Dwight Merriman's ad-targeting software in early 1996, sold banners across a network of sites and served them from one computer [22]. Google bought it in 2008 [23].

Then the market got a number. The IAB's first revenue report, administered by Coopers and Lybrand, counted $267 million of US internet advertising in 1996 [7].

The bust arrived on schedule. Revenue reached $8.2 billion in 2000, then fell 12 per cent in 2001 and 16 per cent in 2002, to $6.0 billion [8][9]. Banners carried the fall: 48 per cent of 2000 revenue, 36 per cent of 2001, while keyword search went from 1 per cent to 4 [8]. By 2008 search was 45 per cent and display-related formats 33 per cent [10].

The click rate collapsed before the money did. Nielsen's figures, as cited by Pagendarm and Schaumburg, put the average banner at 2 per cent in 1995, 0.5 per cent in October 1998 and 0.2 per cent in May 2000 [18]. Nielsen/NetRatings put April 1999 at 0.63 per cent, and its vice president Tim Meadows told Forbes that "click-throughs are a convenient metric to track, but it's not the best one" [19]. DoubleClick's 2009 benchmark for the United States was 0.10 per cent for static ads and 0.09 per cent for Flash [20]. McCambley himself wrote in 2013 that by 1998 the banner was back to "delivering what TV spots, radio spots, and print ads had delivered for years: sales messages" [5].

The banner made attention countable, and what can be counted gets priced. Tim Wu's name for the model HotWired adopted is the attention merchant: a free diversion gathers a crowd, and the crowd is sold to advertisers [31]. That trade is older than the web. What the rectangle added was a meter.

## The Mad Men thread

The agencies the series dramatises were, by 1994, already inside holding companies. Marion Harper of McCann-Erickson created the first, Interpublic, in January 1961, and was forced out by his bankers before the decade ended [24]. In 1986 BBDO, Doyle Dane Bernbach and Needham Harper merged their shareholdings into Omnicom, with DDB, Bernbach's agency, the weakest of the three.

Martin Sorrell bought into a maker of wire shopping baskets in 1985, renamed it WPP, took J. Walter Thompson for $566 million in 1987 and the Ogilvy Group for $864 million in 1989 [25]. David Ogilvy had called him "an odious little shit". WPP made Ogilvy its chairman to calm the clients.

Under all of them sat the 15 per cent media commission, which survived a 1956 consent decree and lasted into the 1980s. It broke in the years around the banner. The share of advertisers who bought media separately from creative went from 18 per cent in 1991 to 47 per cent in 1994, and the share of agencies paid on billings fell from 61 per cent in 1994 to 10 per cent by 2003 [28]. WPP merged the media departments of JWT and Ogilvy into Mindshare in 1997, and the media agency became a business of its own.

The agencies were in the room at HotWired, but as subcontractors. IBM's banner came from Ogilvy in New York, Sprint's from JWT in San Francisco, AT&T's from Modem Media, and Organic, the web shop one floor up, built about half the set [1]. Ad Age called 1994 "the year of the internet" and noted that network television, spot television and magazines still ruled agency billings.

The technology companies took the middle ground the agencies left. DoubleClick was an ad network and an ad server "before anyone knew what those were", and within four years it had 2,000 staff in 25 countries [21].

Ken Auletta is blunt. The flight of advertisers from old to new media started in the late 1990s and accelerated in the new century, while "in the public imagination, we were still in the age of Don Draper" [30].

Our reading is that the commission died of daylight. An agency paid 15 per cent of a television budget earned its margin from the medium's opacity. A banner that reports impressions, clicks and cost per click to the client every morning has no opacity to sell.

The agencies were not emptied, though. US agency employment was 171,000 in 1990, peaked at 203,000 in 2000, fell to 166,000 by 2010 and stood at 209,000 in 2025, across a period in which internet advertising went from nothing to $259 billion [37].

## Applied: if you are a B2C brand

Say you sell running shoes and your display report leads with click-through rate. Most of the reports we are sent do. Three things from the record.

Click-through was high only while nobody had seen a banner before. Anker's floor of 2 per cent held into 1995, and the DoubleClick benchmark fifteen years later was a tenth of one per cent [20].

The click never measured attention. Nielsen's vice president said so in 1999, and Lumen's eye-tracking panel found that a viewable desktop display ad had a 22 per cent chance of being looked at at all, for one to two seconds [35]. Your report cannot tell you whether anyone saw the shoe.

The people who click are the people who were already buying. Byron Sharp's reading of retargeting is that it "works, sometimes" because it nudges someone already halfway through a purchase, and that hyper-targeting as a strategy is "unrealistic thinking" [32]. Binet and Field's analysis of the IPA Databank finds reach accounts for around 83 per cent of the variation in media effectiveness between channels [34].

So judge the display line by reach among category buyers and by what branded search and direct traffic do in the weeks after it runs. Report cost per thousand viewed beside cost per click.

## Applied: if you are a B2B brand

Say you sell enterprise software and your team runs programmatic display to "decision makers". Most of that audience will not buy software this year. Sharp calls advertising to them "a miserable thing to do" on a return-on-investment view, and also the investment that pays in ten years [33].

Attention is a worse number than the click. IAS measured global display viewability at 67.9 per cent in 2025, against 79.7 per cent for video, and found that mobile web display was 45.1 per cent of impressions and 71.9 per cent of the impressions on made-for-advertising sites [36]. In Lumen's desktop panel, between 9 and 22 per cent of ads served, depending on format, ever got a single eye fixation [35].

Buy the large formats on named publishers your buyers read. Cap mobile web display unless you have opened the page from the placement report. Then measure the campaign by whether the accounts you named appear in pipeline. Who clicked goes in the appendix.

## What to do with it

1. Add one column to last quarter's display report for impressions both viewable and looked at, using your verification vendor's time-in-view figure. If the vendor has no such figure, write "not measured". 2. Take click-through rate out of the campaign objectives and keep it as a diagnostic. If a display line shows above 1 per cent today, check it for invalid traffic and accidental taps. 3. Split the same report by format size: 970 by 250, 300 by 600 and 300 by 250 in one group, 320 by 50 and 728 by 90 in the other. Move the next budget towards the first group. 4. Work out the share of digital budget on retargeting. If it is above a fifth, cut it to a fifth and put the difference into reach among non-customers. 5. Compare your 2024 split of search to display with the IAB's 39.8 and 28.7 per cent [14], and write one sentence on why yours differs and whether that is on purpose.

### 2000. Google launches AdWords

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/history-of-advertising/2000-google-adwords/
Date: 2026-08-09. Read: 10 min.

In October 2000 Google let any business buy a search query. The AdWords record, the auction, the commission it bypassed, and what to do with it.

## The moment

Mountain View, California, 23 October 2000. Google is two years old, privately held, answering more than 20 million searches a day, and it puts out a press release [1]. The product is called AdWords. Any business can go to adwords.google.com, pick keywords, write a short text ad, and watch it appear beside the search results within minutes. There is no sales call and no agency in between. Around 350 businesses and agencies signed up during the beta earlier in the month. The ad shows only when a user types the words the advertiser bought; the release calls the result a "prequalified visitor". Nobody calls it the end of the media department.

## What came before

Banner advertising on the web was sold the way magazine pages were, by the thousand impressions, on the hope that the right people were looking. Google's first ads, the premium sponsorships of August 2000, went through a sales team at a cost per thousand, and AdWords at launch kept that logic: $15, $12 and $10 per thousand impressions for the top, middle and bottom positions [1].

The idea that a search engine could auction its results had already been tried, and booed. In February 1998 Bill Gross of the Idealab incubator stood on the TED stage and demonstrated GoTo.com, where advertisers bid for position and paid only when someone clicked. Gross remembered the logic years later: "The whole point of Internet advertising, I thought, was accountability. You could measure it, unlike with print ads." GoTo went public in June 1999, won the AOL syndication deal in September 2000, renamed itself Overture in 2001, and by early 2003 had 88,000 active advertisers [14, 15, 12].

Gross had not patented it, and said so: "We didn't patent the idea. So if we don't patent it, they can copy it." The disputed first is therefore clear enough. Paid placement by auction was Overture's. The self-service keyword ad, matched to a query and bought without a human, was Google's. Google put the two together sixteen months later [14].

## What it changed

On 20 February 2002 Google announced AdWords Select: cost per click instead of cost per thousand, and an auction in which position was set by "a combination of ad performance (click-thru rate) and how much an advertiser agrees to pay per click" [2]. The second clause is the invention. An ad nobody clicked sank however much its owner bid, which made relevance a pricing input.

The day after, a marketer could do three things that had never been possible together. Buy a stated need rather than an audience that might have one. Pay only when the need became a click. Change price, copy and keyword at two in the morning with no insertion order and nobody to take to lunch. Philip Kotler and Kevin Lane Keller describe it in Marketing Management as a "continuous auction on search terms that serve as a proxy for the consumer's product or consumption interests" [25].

The money followed fast. Google's advertising revenue was $66.9 million in 2001, $410.9 million in 2002 and $1.42 billion in 2003, and advertisers supplied 94 to 99 percent of revenue through the first decade [3, 4, 5]. In 2025 Google advertising revenue was $294.7 billion, and Alphabet still took "more than 70% of total revenues from online advertising" [11].

Overture sued in 2002 [14]. Yahoo bought Overture in 2003 for about $1.63 billion [12]. On 9 August 2004, nine days before Google priced its IPO, the two settled: Google took a licence to US Patent 6,269,361, Yahoo dropped the suit, and Google issued 2.7 million Class A shares to Yahoo for the patent and an older warrant dispute [13].

Search became the largest category of US internet advertising and has led it since: 35 percent of the total in 2003, 40 percent in 2004 [16a]. The share has slipped as video and social grew, from 48 percent in 2016 to 38.8 percent in 2025, while the dollars climbed from $34.6 billion to $114.2 billion [16b, 16h].

In 2019 US television advertising was still $70.6 billion against $54.7 billion for paid search, in the same IAB and PwC tables [16d]. By 2021 search had reached $78.3 billion and television, on eMarketer's count, $65.7 billion [16e, 17]. The crossing sits in 2020 or 2021; we could not reach the one table that would settle it.

Google said in October 2000 that it handled more than 20 million searches a day; in August 2012, 100 billion a month; in May 2016, "trillions" a year; in March 2025, "more than 5 trillion searches on Google annually" [1, 20, 21, 19]. One engine has held around nine in ten of the world's searches in every year StatCounter has counted [18].

## The Mad Men thread

Readers who arrive through Mad Men come for the copywriters. The record says the money came from somewhere else. From about 1920 the American media granted recognised agencies a 15 percent commission on the space and time they placed, a rate the American Association of Advertising Agencies had helped fix in 1918; the client paid the gross rate and the agency kept the difference [30, 31].

The commission paid for copy, research, layouts and media planning, as Time explained in February 1956, when a Justice Department consent decree ended the 4As requirement that members collect 15 percent. The rule went; the habit stayed. In 1960 Shell and Ogilvy's agency tried a fee instead of 15 percent and made the New York Times for it [29, 31].

So the 1960s media department earned more when the client spent more. Prices were negotiated between people who knew each other, and nothing in the system rewarded buying less.

Mel Karmazin, then chief executive of Viacom, visited Google in 2003 and heard Page and Brin make the case for measuring everything, including the effectiveness of advertising. Ken Auletta records what Karmazin said on his way out, only half in jest: "You're fucking with the magic!" Auletta's next line is the one to keep. "Engineers don't believe in magic." [22]

The auction did what the consent decree could not. There was no commission to collect and no sales rep to keep sweet, and a client with a credit card could run the account from a laptop. The flight of advertisers from old to new media, Auletta writes in Frenemies, "started in the late 1990s and accelerated in the new century" [23].

The holding companies answered by putting a desk of their own between the client and the exchange: VivaKi at Publicis from 2008, Accuen at Omnicom, Xaxis at WPP's GroupM in June 2011, which Brian Lesser launched as "a new, global audience buying company" [32]. The agency was back in the room, and this time the margin was its own to defend rather than the medium's to grant.

## Applied: if you are a B2C brand

Say you sell a mattress online and search is your largest line. The AdWords record says you are buying intent that already exists. Someone typed "best mattress for back pain" before your ad appeared, and the auction charged you for being there when they did. Les Binet and Peter Field, in the IPA's Media in Focus, found paid search and email the most effective activation channels, and warned that activation effects "tend to decay away quickly, and don't tend to build much over time" [26]. Search harvests what something else planted.

So run two books. In the first, treat every query as a buying situation and manage it like stock: exact and phrase match on the terms that convert, negative keywords for the ones that only cost, and a cost-per-order ceiling you enforce. In the second, accept that how many people search for a mattress this month is set by how many beds are wearing out, and that only brand work changes whose name they type. Kotler and Keller draw the same line, broad terms for brand building and specific ones for leads [25].

We watched it happen on an anonymised residential case, a developer launching a property into a category nobody was searching yet. We built a forty-eight-term keyword architecture in four intent groups, "not to capture demand" but "to find out which door people would come through once demand existed", and kept the paid search money on the established project, where demand was real. Qualified enquiries for the launch grew every month of the quarter. Search spend follows demand and never leads it [33].

## Applied: if you are a B2B brand

Say you sell industrial sensors and your buyers search rarely but specifically. A plant engineer who types "ATEX certified vibration sensor 4-20mA" has told you what she needs, the standard it must meet and the signal it must speak. That query is a specification, and the auction will price it as one. Pay. Write the ad in her words and land her on the datasheet. Measure to the quote request rather than the click.

John Dawes of the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute has the arithmetic for the rest of the budget: firms change providers of services like banking or software "around once every five years on average", so "only 20% of business buyers are 'in the market' over the course of an entire year; something like 5% in a quarter" [27]. The other 95 percent are typing nothing this quarter, and no bid reaches them. Dawes concludes that you advertise to people who are out of the market now, so yours is the name they know when they come in.

So the sensor company runs search narrow, a few hundred exact queries with a cost per lead finance has signed off, and spends the rest on being the name in the engineer's head when the old sensor fails. The thin query is a door. Somebody still has to make her want to walk through yours.

## What to do with it

1. Split the search account into demand you capture (queries people type) and demand you wish existed (queries you hope for), and report them as two lines. If the second line is still spending in month three, move that money to brand work. 2. Pull click-through rate by keyword every month and rewrite or cut the bottom quartile before raising a bid; the auction has priced relevance since 2002. 3. Set one cost-per-enquiry ceiling per intent group and write it into the bid rules, so a competitor's enthusiasm cannot inflate your line. 4. Put a dated number on the share of this quarter's budget that reaches people who are not searching; if it is under half, write down why. 5. Once a year read the IAB and PwC format table and Alphabet's 10-K revenue note; if your search line grows faster than the category, find out who is funding the difference.

### 2022. ChatGPT is released

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/history-of-advertising/2022-chatgpt/
Date: 2026-08-04. Read: 10 min.

ChatGPT, 30 November 2022: the day the answer replaced the results page. What the record shows, what it changed for brands, and what to do on Monday.

## The moment

On 30 November 2022, OpenAI posted a note titled "Introducing ChatGPT". It said the company had trained a model that "interacts in a conversational way", that the dialogue format let it answer follow-up questions and admit its mistakes, and that during the research preview use was free [1]. The launch was that post and a link.

Five days later Sam Altman wrote that ChatGPT had "crossed 1 million users" [2]. The box took anything: a contract, a recipe, a shopping question. Somewhere in that first week a shopper typed a question that would once have gone to a search box, read the paragraph that came back, and did not click anything. That is the moment.

## What came before

A buyer with a question had, since the late 1990s, one habit: type it into a search engine, read a page of links, click two or three, decide. Digital marketing sat on top of that habit, the auction beside the links, the agencies bidding in it, the pages written to rank in it. Tim Wu calls the business the attention merchant, and the deal, in his publisher's summary, has not changed since the penny press: "free diversion in exchange for a moment of your time, sold in turn to the highest-bidding advertiser" [25].

Conversational answers were not new in 2022. Google had shown its own dialogue model, LaMDA, in 2021. On 6 February 2023 Sundar Pichai announced Bard, "an experimental conversational AI service, powered by LaMDA", and opened it to trusted testers [12]. A year later Bard became Gemini. Google had the model first. OpenAI had the product first, free and public, in a chat box, with no instructions.

## What it changed

The day before, a marketer could buy a position on a page and write a page that deserved one. The day after, a model read the pages and wrote the answer itself, named two or three brands in it, and the buyer often stopped there. The brand is either in the answer or it is not. There is no second page.

The UBS note reported by Reuters estimated 100 million monthly users in January 2023, two months after launch; the analysts wrote that "in 20 years following the internet space, we cannot recall a faster ramp in a consumer internet app" [3]. TikTok had taken about nine months and Instagram two and a half years [4]. OpenAI then switched to a stricter measure, weekly active users: 100 million in November 2023, 200 million in August 2024, 300 million in December 2024, 400 million in February 2025, 800 million in October 2025, 900 million in February 2026, and "more than 1 billion" by the end of August 2026 [5][6][7][8][9][10][11].

Google answered inside search itself. On 14 May 2024 Elizabeth Reid wrote that "AI Overviews will begin rolling out to everyone in the U.S." [14]. Semrush tracked more than ten million keywords through 2025 and found the share of US desktop queries triggering an AI Overview went from 6.49% in January to 13.14% in March and 24.61% in July, before settling at 15.69% in November [15]. Google is still deciding how often to show one. Plan for the range.

Then the clicks. Pew Research Center watched 900 US adults make 68,879 Google searches in March 2025. An AI summary appeared on 18% of them, and when it did users clicked a result link on 8% of visits against 15% when it did not, clicked a link inside the summary on 1% of visits, and ended their browsing session 26% of the time against 16% [16]. Gartner had already forecast in February 2024 that traditional search engine volume would drop 25% by 2026 as chatbots and virtual agents took share [18]. Nothing in the sources here says whether it has. Semrush and Pew point the same way.

The money did not leave. US internet advertising revenue went from $209.7 billion in 2022 to $294.6 billion in 2025 [20]. What moved is where a brand gets remembered.

Byron Sharp defines mental availability as "the probability that a buyer will notice, recognize and/or think of a brand in buying situations" [26]. For seventy years that probability lived in the buyer's memory. From 2022 it has a second holder, a model that is asked the buying question and answers from what it has read.

Kevin Lane Keller's measure of breadth, "the range of purchase and consumption situations in which the brand comes to mind" [27], is what an answer engine tests, one prompt at a time. The engine also borrows Robert Cialdini's authority and social proof: it favours sources that combine expertise and trustworthiness, and it repeats what many similar others say [28]. Pew found the summaries drew 15% of their sources from Wikipedia, YouTube and Reddit, and 6% from government sites against 2% in ordinary results [16]. The engine cites the reference and the crowd.

The trade named it within a year. In November 2023 six researchers posted a paper titled "GEO: [Generative Engine Optimization](/ai-marketing/what-is-generative-engine-optimization/)", reporting that changes to a page's content could raise its visibility in generative answers by up to 40% [19]. "AEO", answer engine optimisation, followed in the agency decks. The acronyms are new. The test is Sharp's.

## The Mad Men thread

The series puts the reader in a Madison Avenue office in 1960. The record puts a number on how that office was paid. From the 1880s until the 1980s an American agency earned a 15% commission on the media it bought for its client, a system advertisers challenged for decades and that survived a 1956 antitrust consent decree [22]. The agency wrote the message and was paid for buying the audience, both under one roof. Lasker's Lord and Thomas, Rubicam, Ogilvy, Bernbach's DDB, Burnett and Bates argued about the message and sent the same shape of invoice.

The web broke the invoice once already. On 27 October 1994 HotWired went live with banners from a dozen advertisers, among them AT&T, MCI, Volvo and IBM. The AT&T banner was built by Modem Media, a new shop; several others came from Organic; Ogilvy and Mather held IBM's business by contract. The holding companies bought their way in afterwards. Modem Media was folded into Digitas, and Publicis bought Digitas for $1.3 billion in December 2006 [23].

Ken Auletta's word for what came next is frenemies: "a once comfortable agency business is now assailed by frenemies, companies that both compete and cooperate with them" [24].

The 2023 to 2025 record reads like 1994 with larger numbers. In January 2024 WPP told investors its plans included "annual cash investment of around £250m in proprietary technology to support our AI and data strategy". Publicis announced CoreAI on 25 January 2024, with 300 million euros over three years. Omnicom ran generative AI prompting workshops for its own staff at Cannes in June 2024, and the next January its media group wrote from CES that brands "must rethink marketing for a future where AI, not humans, dictates choices" [21]. As in 1994, the agencies arrived after the buyers and paid to catch up. That is our reading of the dates; the record does not measure the gap.

In 1960 the agency controlled the message and bought the audience. In 2022 the model wrote the answer, and all an agency had left to sell was the work of being worth citing.

## Applied: if you are a B2C brand

Say you sell a premium dry food for older dogs, in three European markets, at twice the supermarket price. A shopper opens an assistant and types "what is the best dry food for a senior dog". Three brands come back with a sentence each.

Your ad budget does not decide which three. The engine assembles its answer from pages it trusts, and four things make a page trustable. First, a definition with a source on it. Your page says what "senior" means for a small breed and a large one, names the veterinary source, and the engine lifts the sentence whole. Then mentions by others, a veterinary association's list, a retailer's buying guide, a forum thread where owners compare notes, because the summaries draw on the reference and the crowd [16], and a homepage is neither. Third, an author with a name: a veterinary nutritionist with a registration on the page is Cialdini's authority in a form a model can read. And data of your own, a feeding trial with its sample size and method.

## Applied: if you are a B2B brand

Say you run cold-chain logistics across Europe and your buyers are procurement leads at pharmaceutical companies. One of them types "which cold-chain providers serve pharma in the Netherlands". The same four tests apply and they are harder, because B2B pages are written for a committee that already knows you, and the engine is a stranger with one question. Your definition is the temperature bands and the regulation you ship under, in one sentence. The mentions sit in dull places: the port's directory, the trade body's member list, the pharma association's supplier register, a named article in a trade journal. Put the operations director's name on the page as author. Publish lane-level performance data of your own, with dates.

We have done this to ourselves: on 27 September 2026, a one-sample baseline on one engine, grounding on, four prompts. On the three category prompts, one on agencies a B2B company should hire for [AI marketing](/ai-marketing/what-is-ai-marketing/) and two on investor communications agencies in two markets, the engine named around ten firms per answer. It named no agency we would call a peer, and it named us zero times. The fourth prompt asked who we are, and it described us accurately from our own site [30]. Ask it who we are and it knows. Ask it who to hire and we are not on the list. The dog food brand has the same gap.

## What to do with it

1. Write the ten questions a buyer would type, in their words, and ask each engine you care about once a month. Record three things per answer: named or not, position, and whether the description matches yours. Keep the log. 2. Put a named author with a checkable credential on every page that answers a question, and give each of them one definition the engine can lift in a single sentence. 3. Publish one piece of original data a quarter, with method and sample size. It is the only thing in your category a competitor cannot paste. 4. Count where others mention you in the sources the engines already cite: reference sites, association lists, forums, trade press, government registers. Add one a month. 5. Hold the brand budget. Binet and Field's split, roughly 60:40 brand to activation, was about memory before an engine existed [29]. The engine tests the same memory. Do not fund a new acronym by cutting the thing it measures.

## 03 Branding

How brands are built and how the brain receives them: brand strategy, brand equity, and the neuromarketing studies that are documented.

### The Coke and Pepsi brain study (the Pepsi paradox)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/branding/the-coke-pepsi-study/
Date: 2026-09-06. Read: 4 min.

McClure and colleagues, Neuron, 2004. Told which cola they were drinking, people's stated preference and their brain activity both changed. The brand did the work the taste did not.

The study, from Read Montague's lab at Baylor College of Medicine, ran blind and labelled taste tests inside an fMRI scanner. In the blind condition preferences split. With the Coke label visible, preference shifted toward Coke and activity changed in regions associated with memory and self-image.

It is the most cited demonstration that a brand is a stored pattern in the buyer, not a property of the product.

### System 1 and System 2 thinking in marketing

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/branding/system-1-and-system-2/
Date: 2026-09-02. Read: 3 min.

Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow, 2011. Most decisions, including most purchases, run on the fast, automatic system, and the slow one mostly rationalises afterwards.

Kahneman's book summarised decades of research with Amos Tversky. System 1 is fast, associative and effortless. System 2 is slow, deliberate and lazy.

For a brand the implication is blunt. What feels familiar is decided before the argument is heard. The argument arrives later, to justify it.

### The somatic marker hypothesis

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/branding/somatic-markers/
Date: 2026-08-26. Read: 3 min.

Antonio Damasio, Descartes' Error, 1994. Emotion is part of the machinery of choosing, not noise laid over reason. Patients who lost it could not decide.

Damasio studied patients with damage to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex. Their reasoning was intact and their decision making collapsed. His explanation: the body's emotional signals mark options as good or bad before deliberation starts.

Advertising that produces a feeling is making the argument in the channel the brain uses.

### Where the word came from

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/branding/where-the-word-came-from/
Date: 2026-08-20. Read: 2 min.

The term neuromarketing is commonly credited to Ale Smidts of Erasmus University in Rotterdam, in 2002.

The field grew out of consumer neuroscience in the early 2000s, when brain imaging became cheap enough to point at advertising. Much of what has been sold under the label since is thinner than the founding studies. This section sticks to the documented ones.

### Processing fluency in marketing

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/branding/processing-fluency-in-marketing/
Date: 2026-08-15. Read: 3 min.

Things that are easy to read, see and say are judged more true and more likeable. Reber, Schwarz and Winkielman set the effect out in 2004.

The ease with which the brain processes a stimulus is itself read as a signal. Clear names, legible type, repeated shapes and short claims feel more true than the same content made harder. The brain is grading the effort, not the content.

It is the scientific case for consistency, and against cleverness that costs the reader effort.

### Loss aversion in marketing

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/branding/loss-aversion-in-marketing/
Date: 2026-08-10. Read: 3 min.

Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory, 1979. Losses weigh roughly twice as much as gains of the same size. Most urgency in marketing borrows from this.

Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk was published in Econometrica in 1979. The asymmetry it describes underlies deadlines, free trials that expire and the framing of what a buyer stands to lose by not acting.

Used honestly it clarifies stakes. Used carelessly it trains people to distrust the brand.

## 04 AI marketing

What AI marketing, AI SEO, generative engine optimization and answer engine optimization mean, and what changes for a brand when the buyer asks a model instead of a search engine.

### What is AI marketing?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/what-is-ai-marketing/
Date: 2026-09-14. Read: 3 min.

AI marketing is the use of AI systems in marketing work: to research buyers, generate and test creative, target and bid, and to earn a place in the answers AI assistants give when buyers ask for a recommendation.

The phrase covers two different jobs that often get mixed together. The first is using AI inside the marketing team: research, drafting, audience models, bidding, personalisation, reporting. The second is marketing to AI: making sure the systems buyers now ask can find the company, name it and describe it correctly.

The second job is the newer one. ChatGPT was released on 30 November 2022, and asking a model for a shortlist has since become a normal step before a purchase. That step happens before the buyer reaches anyone's website, which is why it belongs to marketing rather than to a tools budget.

Most of what is sold as AI marketing is the first job. Most of what changes a company's pipeline is the second. The entries in this section cover the terms used for it: [AI SEO](/ai-marketing/what-is-ai-seo/), [generative engine optimization](/ai-marketing/what-is-generative-engine-optimization/), [answer engine optimization](/ai-marketing/what-is-answer-engine-optimization/), and retrievable brands.

### What is generative engine optimization (GEO)?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/what-is-generative-engine-optimization/
Date: 2026-09-13. Read: 3 min.

Generative engine optimization, or GEO, is the practice of writing and structuring content so that generative engines cite it in the answers they produce. The term comes from a 2023 research paper by Pranjal Aggarwal and colleagues.

The paper, GEO: Generative Engine Optimization, was posted to arXiv in November 2023 by Pranjal Aggarwal, Vishvak Murahari, Tanmay Rajpurohit, Ashwin Kalyan, Karthik Narasimhan and Ameet Deshpande. It introduced the term and a benchmark for testing which changes to a source make it more likely to be used in a generated answer. The authors reported visibility gains of up to 40 per cent on that benchmark.

The practical reading: a generative engine assembles an answer and decides which sources to lean on, instead of ranking pages for a click. So write the sentence you want quoted, put the source next to it, and stop optimising for a position the answer never shows.attributes it, and puts a quotable sentence next to a source gives the engine something it can reuse.

GEO overlaps with SEO at the base, because a page still has to be reachable and readable. It separates on the goal: a position in a list, or a sentence in an answer.

### What is answer engine optimization (AEO)?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/what-is-answer-engine-optimization/
Date: 2026-09-11. Read: 3 min.

Answer engine optimization, or AEO, is the practice of preparing content so that it is used in a direct answer rather than a list of links. In practice it means answering one question per page, plainly and early.

AEO grew out of the years when search engines began answering questions on the results page itself, through featured snippets and knowledge panels. Publishers learned one habit from that period: one question, one clear answer, one page. It transferred to AI assistants without much translation.one clear answer per page, transferred straight to AI assistants.

The mechanics are unglamorous. Use the question as the heading, in the words people type. Answer it in the first two or three sentences. Keep the answer self-contained so it still makes sense when it is lifted out of the page. Put a date, an author and a source on it.

AEO and GEO are now used almost interchangeably. Where people separate them, AEO is about the direct answer and GEO about the generated one. The work is the same work.

### What is AI SEO?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/what-is-ai-seo/
Date: 2026-09-10. Read: 3 min.

AI SEO means two things: using AI tools to do SEO work faster, and optimising a site so that AI search features and assistants surface it. The second is the one that decides whether a brand appears in an answer.

The first meaning is a workflow question. Keyword clustering, drafting, internal linking and schema generation done with AI assistance. It saves hours and changes nothing about what a site deserves to be returned for.

The second meaning is the strategic one. Search results now carry AI-generated summaries above the links, and some buyers ask an assistant instead of opening a results page at all. Being in the ten blue links and being in the summary above them are two different outcomes.

What serves the second meaning: pages built around one question, definitions placed early, structured data, a visible author and date, and a company description that reads the same everywhere it appears. None of that is new SEO advice. It matters more when the output is one paragraph instead of ten links.

### What is a retrievable brand?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/what-is-a-retrievable-brand/
Date: 2026-09-08. Read: 3 min.

A retrievable brand is one that AI assistants and search engines can find, name and describe correctly when a buyer asks. It is built from clear definitions, named frameworks, sourced facts and one consistent description repeated everywhere.

A model answering a question about a category assembles what it can retrieve about each company: the site, the listings, the coverage, the profiles. Contradictions between those sources do not rank lower. They get averaged into something vague, or dropped.

Retrievability is a term from information retrieval, the research field behind search engines, for how easily a document can be surfaced by a system. Leif Azzopardi and Vishwa Vinay proposed it as a measure in 2008. Applied to a brand it asks a blunter question: when a buyer asks for the category, does the name come back.

Brave New, which publishes the Hive, uses retrievable brand as the name of its method. The pillars are short: one definition repeated word for word, a named framework the model can attribute, sourced claims, a visible author and date, and machine-readable structure.

### How do AI models choose which brands to recommend?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/how-ai-models-choose-brands/
Date: 2026-09-06. Read: 4 min.

Models answer from what they were trained on and what they can retrieve at the moment of the question. A brand gets named when it is described the same way across many independent sources and is easy to quote.

Nobody outside the providers can see the weighting, and they do not publish it. What is observable is the pattern in the answers: the brands that come back are described the same way in many places, by sources the system treats as reliable. That is inference rather than documentation, and it is worth saying so.consistently in many places, by sources the system treats as reliable.

Two mechanisms are at work. Training gives the model a rough map of a category from what was on the public web when it was built. Retrieval at question time pulls current pages and cites them. A brand missing from both is not in the running.

The practical consequence is that third-party coverage does more work than site copy. A company can call itself the leading provider on its own homepage as often as it likes. The model is counting how many other sources put it in that category.

It also explains why a rebrand or a change of category costs more than it used to. The old description stays on the web, and it keeps being counted.

### How do I get my company mentioned in ChatGPT and Perplexity answers?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/get-mentioned-in-chatgpt-and-perplexity/
Date: 2026-09-04. Read: 4 min.

Publish a plain definition of what you do, keep that description identical everywhere it appears, earn coverage on the sources the engines already cite, and make your pages easy to read, date and attribute. Then check the answers monthly.

Start by finding out what the engines say now. Write down the ten questions a buyer would actually type, ask each engine, and record three things: whether you are named, where in the answer, and whether the description is right. That is the baseline, and it takes an afternoon.

Then look at what the answers cite. The sources that keep appearing for your category are the ones worth being in: trade publications, directories, association pages, well-kept reference sites. Being described correctly there moves the answer more than another post on your own blog.

On your own site the work is mechanical. One question per page. The answer in the first sixty words. A visible author and date. Schema markup. The same company description in every profile, listing and bio you control.

Then repeat the check on a fixed schedule. Answers move as the sources move, and a single reading tells you nothing about direction.

### What is llms.txt?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/what-is-llms-txt/
Date: 2026-09-03. Read: 2 min.

llms.txt is a plain text file placed at the root of a website that gives AI systems a short, curated summary of the site and links to its most useful pages. Jeremy Howard of Answer.AI proposed it in 2024.

The reasoning behind the proposal: a model reading a web page has a limited context window and has to wade through navigation, scripts and styling to reach the content. A markdown file at /llms.txt hands it the short version instead.

The format is simple. The site name as a heading, a short description, then linked sections with a line of context for each. Some sites also publish llms-full.txt, which carries the full content as markdown.

It is a proposed convention rather than a standard, and no model provider is obliged to read it. It costs about an hour to write. The useful side effect is that writing one forces a company to say plainly what it does and which pages matter.

### Why does brand consistency matter for AI search?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/ai-marketing/why-brand-consistency-matters-for-ai-search/
Date: 2026-09-01. Read: 3 min.

Because a model reads every version of your company that exists online and averages them. Three different descriptions produce a vague answer or no answer. One description, repeated exactly, produces a sentence the model can quote.

Consistency used to be a design argument about logos and tone of voice. It is now a retrieval argument. The old directory entry, the abandoned profile, the press release from the last positioning, the conference bio written in a hurry: a model weighs all of them alongside the current homepage.

The fix is unglamorous and finite. Write one entity statement, a sentence or two saying what the company is, who it serves and where. Then replace the description everywhere it appears: the site, the schema, every social profile, every directory, every author bio, every partner page.

Marketers resist this because repeating the same sentence feels lazy. It is the opposite. Variation is the part the writer enjoys and the part the machine cannot use.

## 05 Reputation

What a reputation is, how it differs from a brand, how trust is measured, and what the documented cases teach about keeping it.

### Brand versus reputation: what is the difference?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/reputation/brand-versus-reputation/
Date: 2026-09-14. Read: 3 min.

A brand is what a company says and shows about itself. A reputation is what others conclude from what it does. One is authored, the other is earned, and in a buying meeting the second one decides.

Brand is the set of promises and signals a company controls: its name, its claims, its design, its tone. Reputation is the judgement held by people the company does not control: customers, employees, journalists, regulators, and now the models that read all of them.

The two drift apart when the promise outruns the behaviour. That gap is where crises start, and it is the first thing an institutional buyer checks before signing anything.

### The Edelman Trust Barometer

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/reputation/the-edelman-trust-barometer/
Date: 2026-09-12. Read: 3 min.

An annual survey of trust in business, government, media and NGOs, published by Edelman every year since 2001. It is the most cited public measure of institutional trust.

The barometer surveys tens of thousands of respondents across more than twenty countries each year, and reports trust in the four institutions and in specific sectors. The finding that keeps repeating: business is the institution people trust most, and people expect companies to act on issues governments have not. It measures belief rather than behaviour, which is worth holding on to.

Read the current year's report rather than a summary of it. The numbers move, the headlines about them lag.

### 1982. The Tylenol case

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/reputation/the-tylenol-case-1982/
Date: 2026-09-10. Read: 3 min.

After seven people in the Chicago area died from cyanide-laced Tylenol capsules, Johnson & Johnson recalled the product nationwide and introduced tamper-evident packaging. It remains the reference case in crisis communications.

The company recalled about 31 million bottles, stopped advertising, communicated openly with the press and the public, and relaunched the product in tamper-resistant packaging within months. Market share recovered.

The lesson taught in every crisis course since: act on the public's safety before the balance sheet, say what you know when you know it, and let the packaging carry the promise afterwards.

### What is trust architecture?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/reputation/trust-architecture/
Date: 2026-09-08. Read: 3 min.

Trust architecture is the deliberate arrangement of proof around a company so that a buyer, a journalist or a model can verify its claims without asking. At Brave New it is the name of that discipline.

Proof is the evidence a claim needs to survive procurement: named clients, audited numbers, dated results, people who can be called. Architecture is putting that proof where it will be found, in the order a sceptical reader checks it.

A brand that asserts and a reputation that is verified are different assets. The second one moves the multiple.

### What is reputation risk?

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/reputation/reputation-risk/
Date: 2026-09-06. Read: 2 min.

Reputation risk is the chance that an event, a decision or a disclosure changes what stakeholders believe about a company, and with it the company's ability to sell, hire, borrow or be regulated on the same terms.

Unlike operational or financial risk it rarely arrives alone. It is the second-order effect of another failure, and it compounds when the company's first statements turn out to be wrong.

The control that works is closing the distance between what a company claims in public and what it can prove on request. A crisis plan in a drawer does much less.

## 06 Readings

Check our readings. The books we like, what each one argues, and one line worth keeping from each.

### How Brands Grow. Byron Sharp (2010)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/readings/how-brands-grow-byron-sharp/
Date: 2026-09-13. Read: 3 min.

The evidence-based case that brands grow by reaching more buyers, not by deepening loyalty. Built on decades of purchase data from the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute.

> Growth comes from being easy to think of and easy to buy, not from being loved by a few.

Sharp sets out laws that hold across categories: brands with more buyers also have slightly more loyal buyers, most of a brand's sales come from light buyers, and competing brands share customers in proportion to their size. The practical conclusion is mental availability, physical availability and distinctive assets.

It is the book to read before any loyalty programme is proposed. Most of the marketing that feels clever runs against the data in it.

### Ogilvy on Advertising. David Ogilvy (1983)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/readings/ogilvy-on-advertising/
Date: 2026-09-11. Read: 3 min.

The working manual of the man who built Ogilvy & Mather, on headlines, layouts, research and the difference between advertising that wins awards and advertising that sells.

> The consumer is not a moron. Write as if she were reading over your shoulder.

Ogilvy writes from the agency floor: what he tested, what worked, and what he refused to do. The chapters on headlines, long copy and research are still the plainest instruction on the trade in print.

Read it for the discipline. The examples are old; the standards are not.

### Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind. Al Ries and Jack Trout (1981)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/readings/positioning-ries-and-trout/
Date: 2026-09-09. Read: 3 min.

The book that moved the battleground from the product to the prospect's mind. Own a word, or a place relative to the leader, before someone else does.

> You do not position a product. You position it in a mind that is already full.

Ries and Trout argue that the mind rejects what does not fit what it already knows, so the job is to find an open position and hold it. Being second is fine if you say so; being a copy of the leader is fatal.

Short, repetitive, and still the origin of the word every strategy deck uses without credit.

### Thinking, Fast and Slow. Daniel Kahneman (2011)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/readings/thinking-fast-and-slow-kahneman/
Date: 2026-09-07. Read: 4 min.

Kahneman's summary of forty years of research with Amos Tversky on how judgement works in practice: two systems, one fast and automatic, one slow and lazy.

> Most buying is decided before the argument is heard.

The book covers anchoring, loss aversion, framing, the availability heuristic and the planning fallacy, with the experiments that established each. For marketers it is the source text under most of what is sold as neuromarketing.

Long, and worth reading in full once. After that, the Branding section here is the short version.

### The Long and the Short of It. Les Binet and Peter Field (2013)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/readings/the-long-and-the-short-of-it-binet-field/
Date: 2026-09-05. Read: 2 min.

The IPA study of what produced measurable business effects across hundreds of campaigns: brand building and sales activation work on different timescales and need different creative.

> Activation pays this quarter. Brand pays every quarter after.

Binet and Field analysed the IPA Effectiveness Databank and found that campaigns balancing long-term brand building with short-term activation outperformed campaigns that did either alone. The much-quoted 60 to 40 split comes from here.

A thin report rather than a book, and the most cited document in effectiveness planning.

### Alchemy. Rory Sutherland (2019)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/readings/alchemy-rory-sutherland/
Date: 2026-09-03. Read: 3 min.

Sutherland's argument that the most valuable ideas in business do not survive a spreadsheet, because people do not choose the way economics assumes they do.

> The opposite of a good idea can also be a good idea.

The book collects cases where a change in perception did the work a change in product could not, and argues for testing the illogical alongside the logical. It is behavioural economics written by a practitioner rather than a professor.

Read it when the plan is rational, complete and somehow not working.

### Influence. Robert Cialdini (1984)

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/readings/influence-cialdini/
Date: 2026-09-01. Read: 3 min.

Cialdini's six principles of persuasion, reciprocity, commitment, social proof, authority, liking and scarcity, each traced to the research and the compliance professionals who use it.

> Every persuasion technique is a shortcut the brain already takes.

The book was written to help people resist persuasion and became the manual for practising it. The chapters on social proof and scarcity explain most of what happens on a landing page.

Later editions add a seventh principle, unity. The original six are enough.

## 07 Research

Original studies from the Hive: how AI engines answer marketing questions, what people type into a search box, and what that means for a brand. Every number comes from a named tool on a stated date.

### How AI engines answer marketing questions: a citation study

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/research/how-ai-engines-answer-marketing-questions/
Date: 2026-09-14. Read: 5 min.

We asked a live AI engine eight marketing questions and checked every source it named. For six of the eight it never searched, and 21 of the 52 sources it listed do not exist.

Method: eight questions covering marketing principles, the history of advertising, neuromarketing, AI search, films and songs about advertising, marketing reference sites and the term [retrievable brand](/ai-marketing/what-is-a-retrievable-brand/), put to Gemini with Google Search grounding on 14 September 2026, one answer each. Every URL the engine named was requested and its status recorded.

Finding one: live retrieval fired only for the two questions about AI search and marketing reference sites. The evergreen questions were answered from training data, so the sources listed were the model's memory of the web rather than anything it had just read. Twenty-one of fifty-two returned not found. That was the number that surprised us.

Finding two: on the questions where the engine did search, it cited platform vendors, trade publications and several small, recently published explainer posts side by side. A new page can enter those answers within an update cycle. A new page on an evergreen topic cannot, whatever its quality.

What it means: publish the pages on contested, fresh topics first. Treat evergreen reference pages as a search engine play. Verify every citation an engine gives you before repeating it. Limits: one engine, one sample per question. We will repeat the study on other engines and publish the differences.

Figure: Sources an AI engine named, checked one by one. 52 URLs listed across six questions answered without live search. Source: Gemini with Google Search grounding, one answer per question, 14 Sep 2026; each URL requested by hand. Unit: URLs.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Exist | 17 |
| Blocked the check, unverified | 14 |
| Do not exist | 21 |

### How the AI search vocabulary moved in a year

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/research/how-the-ai-search-vocabulary-moved/
Date: 2026-09-14. Read: 4 min.

Three terms for the same worry, tracked month by month. AI marketing spiked and settled, generative engine optimization drifted down from its peak, and answer engine optimization held flat at a lower level.

Method: US monthly search volume for three phrases from Ubersuggest, fetched on 14 September 2026, covering August 2025 to July 2026. The phrases are the three names the market uses for getting a brand into AI answers.

[AI marketing](/ai-marketing/what-is-ai-marketing/) is the largest and the most volatile: 9,900 in September 2025, then a slide to 3,600 by May 2026. [Generative engine optimization](/ai-marketing/what-is-generative-engine-optimization/) started the period at 6,600 and finished at 4,400. [Answer engine optimization](/ai-marketing/what-is-answer-engine-optimization/) never left the 1,900 to 2,900 band.

Reading: the general phrase collects curiosity and then loses it, while the specialist phrases hold a smaller, steadier audience of people who already know what they need. The practical use of that is dull. Put the general name in the title, the specialist names in the headings, and both readers land on the same page.

Limits: one tool, one country, twelve months. We will add other countries and repeat the pull each quarter so the lines get longer.

Figure: How the AI search vocabulary moved. US monthly searches, Aug 2025 to Jul 2026. Source: Ubersuggest, US, fetched 14 Sep 2026. Unit: searches per month.

| Month | AI marketing | Generative engine optimization | Answer engine optimization |
|---|---|---|---|
| Aug 25 | 5,400 | 6,600 | 2,400 |
| Sep 25 | 9,900 | 6,600 | 2,900 |
| Oct 25 | 6,600 | 5,400 | 2,400 |
| Nov 25 | 5,400 | 4,400 | 2,400 |
| Dec 25 | 4,400 | 3,600 | 1,900 |
| Jan 26 | 5,400 | 5,400 | 1,900 |
| Feb 26 | 4,400 | 4,400 | 1,900 |
| Mar 26 | 5,400 | 5,400 | 2,900 |
| Apr 26 | 4,400 | 3,600 | 2,400 |
| May 26 | 3,600 | 3,600 | 2,400 |
| Jun 26 | 3,600 | 3,600 | 2,400 |
| Jul 26 | 3,600 | 4,400 | 2,400 |

### What people search for in marketing: the demand map

Source: https://bravenewhive.com/research/what-people-search-for-in-marketing/
Date: 2026-09-14. Read: 4 min.

US monthly search volumes for the topics a marketing reference site might cover. The concept names win, the author names do not, and two categories we planned barely exist as searches.

Method: section names and entry titles for this site were checked in Ubersuggest for US monthly volume and difficulty on 14 September 2026, with short-form demand checked in Virlo over the previous ninety days.

Concept phrasing carries the demand: marketing mix 14,800 searches a month, the [4 Ps of marketing](/principles/4-ps-of-marketing/) 12,100, [market segmentation](/principles/market-segmentation/) 9,900, [positioning in marketing](/principles/positioning-in-marketing/) 9,900, loss aversion 8,100. The same ideas searched by author name get almost nothing: positioning Ries Trout 50, Binet and Field 30.

Category names matter as much. History of advertising draws 720 against history of marketing at 210. Movies about advertising draws 1,300 against movies about marketing at 590. Branding in the age of AI draws 10; [AI marketing](/ai-marketing/what-is-ai-marketing/) draws 5,400 and [AI SEO](/ai-marketing/what-is-ai-seo/) 8,100. Songs about marketing draws 70, which is why that section exists for the reader who finds it, not for search.

Short-form video shows the same pattern. The marketing hashtag had 4,234 videos and 140 million views in ninety days; advertising history had six videos averaging 81,000 views each. Demand with almost no supply. We renamed three sections and most entry titles on the strength of numbers like these, which is more deference to a keyword tool than we would usually admit.

Figure: Concept names win, author names do not. US monthly searches for the same idea, two phrasings. Source: Ubersuggest, US, fetched 14 Sep 2026. Unit: searches per month.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Marketing mix | 14,800 |
| 4 Ps of marketing | 12,100 |
| Market segmentation | 9,900 |
| Positioning in marketing | 9,900 |
| Loss aversion | 8,100 |
| Positioning Ries Trout | 50 |
| Binet and Field | 30 |

Figure: Two evergreen topics over a year. US monthly searches, Jul 2025 to Jul 2026. Source: Ubersuggest, US, fetched 14 Sep 2026. Unit: searches per month.
